If anything, the bigger risk with succulents generally is overwatering rather than underwatering, so erring on the side of waiting a bit longer rather than a bit less is almost always the safer call. Once the week's up, water thoroughly until it drains from the bottom, then let the soil dry out mostly before watering again going forward.

There's this savings challenge trend going around where you save a different small increasing amount each week for a year, and my sister is really into it and posting her progress constantly. Do these viral savings challenges actually help people save more, or is it mostly performative posting?

how are octopuses so smart despite being so different from vertebrates neurologically?

Octopus intelligence is a striking case of convergent evolution - complex cognition evolving independently along a completely separate evolutionary branch from vertebrates. Roughly two-thirds of an octopus's neurons aren't even in its central brain, they're distributed throughout its eight arms, giving each arm a significant degree of autonomous sensory processing and even localized decision-making, so an octopus can have an arm exploring a crevice and reacting to what it touches somewhat independently of the central brain's direct moment-to-moment control. This decentralized architecture is fundamentally different from the vertebrate model of a central brain issuing top-down commands through a spinal cord. Despite that structural difference, octopuses demonstrate behaviors associated with high intelligence in vertebrates - they can solve novel puzzles like unscrewing jar lids to get food, use tools such as carrying coconut shells for shelter, and show individual personality differences and apparent play behavior, all without anything resembling a vertebrate brain's architecture.
is there a leading theory for why that level of intelligence would evolve in a solitary short-lived animal?

This is actually one of the more debated puzzles in the field, since the usual evolutionary explanations for intelligence in vertebrates - long lifespans allowing learning to pay off, complex social structures requiring social cognition - largely don't apply to octopuses, which are mostly solitary and live only one to a few years. The leading hypothesis centers on their soft, shell-less bodies leaving them extremely vulnerable, which likely drove intense selective pressure for behavioral flexibility, camouflage strategies, and rapid problem-solving to evade predators and exploit varied food sources, essentially substituting cognitive flexibility for the physical armor or speed that many other prey animals rely on instead. It's considered a strong example of intelligence arising from ecological necessity and predation pressure rather than from the social or long-lifespan pathways that typically get discussed in vertebrate contexts.
I've signed up for my first marathon, it's in 16 weeks. I can currently comfortably run about 6 miles. Is 16 weeks enough time and what should the overall shape of a training plan look like?

16 weeks is a solid, fairly standard timeframe for a first marathon starting from a 6 mile comfortable base, this is actually right in the typical range most beginner marathon plans assume as a starting fitness level, so you're in a good position, not behind at all. The overall shape of a good plan follows a few key principles rather than a rigid specific schedule. Weekly mileage should build gradually, roughly 10% increase per week as a rough ceiling, with a "cutback" week roughly every third or fourth week where mileage drops back down noticeably, this pattern of build-build-build-recover prevents the accumulated fatigue that causes most beginner injuries, which come overwhelmingly from too much volume increase too fast rather than from the marathon distance itself. Your long run is the centerpiece of the whole plan, it should be the longest run of your week every single week, increasing gradually most weeks but also getting cutback treatment periodically, building from something like 8-9 miles in the next couple weeks up toward a peak long run of 20-22 miles around 3 weeks before race day, then tapering down significantly in the final 2-3 weeks to arrive at the start line recovered rather than exhausted. Beyond the long run, most beginner plans include 3-4 total runs per week (an easy run, sometimes a tempo or speed session as you get more experienced, and the long run) with rest or cross-training days between, rather than running every single day, which tends to cause overuse injuries in first-time marathoners specifically.

That's a really intuitive assumption but it actually runs backwards from how the physiology works, and it's one of the most well-established principles in endurance training, so it's worth understanding why rather than just taking it on faith. The key insight is that the actual fitness-building adaptation from a hard training block, stronger muscles, improved cardiovascular efficiency, better fat utilization, doesn't happen during the workout itself, it happens during the recovery period afterward, as your body repairs and adapts to the stress you placed on it. If you keep piling on high volume right up to race day, you're accumulating fatigue faster than your body can complete those adaptations, meaning you arrive at the start line carrying unresolved fatigue on top of whatever fitness you've built, rather than arriving with that fitness fully absorbed and available. The taper specifically works by keeping some running frequency and even some intensity in the final weeks, so your legs stay sharp and you don't lose fitness, while dramatically cutting overall volume, giving your body the dedicated recovery window to finally convert weeks of accumulated training stress into usable, available fitness. Research and decades of practical experience across the sport consistently show runners who taper properly perform better on race day than runners who kept pushing high volume until the very end, even though it feels counterintuitive while you're doing it, there's actually a well-documented psychological phenomenon called "taper madness" where runners feel restless, anxious, or like they're losing fitness during this period precisely because it feels so different from the training you've gotten used to, but the physiological data doesn't support that anxious feeling, trust the taper even when it feels wrong in the moment.

why does caffeine hit some people way harder than others even at the same dose?

A big factor is genetic variation in the CYP1A2 enzyme, which does most of the metabolic work of breaking caffeine down in the liver. People with certain gene variants are fast metabolizers, clearing caffeine from their bloodstream relatively quickly, while others are slow metabolizers, meaning caffeine and its byproducts linger in their system much longer at higher concentrations for the same dose, intensifying and prolonging effects like jitteriness or disrupted sleep. Beyond genetics, regular habitual caffeine use leads to a degree of tolerance, since the brain adapts to chronic caffeine exposure by upregulating adenosine receptors, the receptors caffeine blocks to produce its alertness effect, meaning a habitual heavy coffee drinker often needs more caffeine to get the same subjective jolt that a rare user gets from a much smaller amount. Body weight, other medications competing for the same liver enzymes, and even factors like pregnancy, which substantially slows caffeine clearance, also contribute to the wide variation people experience.

Yes, that's a well-documented effect. Compounds in tobacco smoke induce, meaning they increase the activity of, the same CYP1A2 enzyme responsible for caffeine metabolism, which means smokers often metabolize caffeine roughly twice as fast as non-smokers. This is actually a clinically relevant consideration - when someone quits smoking, their caffeine metabolism slows back down over the following weeks as CYP1A2 activity normalizes, so if they keep drinking the same amount of coffee they were used to as a smoker, they can end up with noticeably higher caffeine levels and increased jitteriness or anxiety than they're used to, which is sometimes mistaken for a symptom of nicotine withdrawal itself rather than a secondary effect of changed caffeine clearance.

Can you explain why my Python generator function only yields values once and then stops even though I call it in a loop?

That's a classic gotcha. A generator object is exhausted after you iterate through it fully once - once the internal state hits StopIteration, it won't reset itself. If you're doing something like gen = my_generator() outside a loop and then reusing gen across multiple outer iterations, the second time through it just yields nothing because it's already spent. The fix is usually to call my_generator() fresh each time you need a new iteration, or convert it to a list if you need to reuse the values repeatedly (though that defeats the memory-saving point of generators). Another common cause is accidentally putting the yield inside a conditional that only fires once - worth checking the loop structure inside the generator itself too.

Not directly on a plain generator, but a common pattern is wrapping it with itertools.tee to create two independent copies, or building a small peekable wrapper class that calls next() once, stashes the value, and returns it on the actual next call. Some libraries like more-itertools ship a peekable class that does exactly this out of the box if you don't want to roll your own.

I'm writing a fantasy novel and my villain currently just feels like generic "wants power for power's sake" evil. How do I make him feel like a real, three dimensional character instead of a cardboard cutout?

The fastest fix for a generic power-hungry villain is usually giving him a goal that's actually sympathetic or at least internally coherent from his own point of view, since the flattest villains are the ones who exist purely as an obstacle for the hero, with wanting-power-for-its-own-sake being basically the laziest version of this, it explains nothing about why he specifically wants it or what he'd actually do with it once achieved. Every genuinely compelling villain, think Killmonger, Thanos, even Darth Vader by the prequels, has a version of events in which they are the protagonist and their actions are justified, often even noble, from inside their own logic, the reader or viewer just happens to disagree with their methods or their read on the situation, not necessarily with their underlying goal. Ask yourself: what does your villain believe is broken about the world, and what personal history convinced him of that belief? Maybe he watched a previous ruler's weakness or mercy directly cause a tragedy, and now genuinely believes that strength and control, even brutal control, prevents worse suffering than kindness ever could, that's a coherent worldview a reader can understand even while rooting against him. Give him a moment, even a small one, of genuine care, humor, or vulnerability directed at someone, a loyal subordinate, a memory of someone he lost, since villains who are capable of real feeling toward at least one person read as far more human and threatening than ones who are cruel indiscriminately to everyone including their own allies.
That's helpful. Should his worldview actually be partially correct, like should the hero have to admit he has a point about something?

Yes, and this is often what separates a good villain from a great one, giving him a piece of truth the hero has to genuinely reckon with, rather than a worldview that's simply wrong and eventually disproven by the plot, creates real thematic tension that elevates the whole story beyond a straightforward good-versus-evil structure. The key craft element here is being precise about which part of his worldview is right and which part is wrong, since making him entirely correct risks making the hero's opposition feel arbitrary or even wrong-headed, while making him entirely incorrect just recreates the flat villain problem you started with in a slightly more dressed up form. A common and effective structure: the villain correctly diagnoses a real problem (say, the previous ruling system truly was corrupt, or truly did fail vulnerable people, or truly was too slow and indecisive to prevent tragedy) but proposes a solution that trades that problem for a worse one (order bought through fear and control that ultimately causes more suffering than the disorder it replaced, or protection that comes at the cost of everyone's freedom or individuality). This lets your hero, and your reader, sit with genuine discomfort, agreeing with the villain's critique of the world while still rejecting his prescription for fixing it, which is a much more interesting position than simple moral clarity. Practically, look for at least one scene where the hero has no good rebuttal in the moment, maybe they change the subject, or deflect, or simply say "there has to be another way" without being able to fully articulate what that way is yet, since a hero who can perfectly counter every villain argument makes the villain retroactively seem less threatening intellectually, while one who's genuinely rattled by a point makes the philosophical conflict feel real and high stakes rather than a foregone conclusion.

My cousin keeps telling me I'm missing out by not putting money into crypto, and honestly I just don't get the appeal beyond speculation. Am I being too closed minded about this or is skepticism the reasonable default here?

Anecdotes about big winners are memorable precisely because they're rare, not because they're representative of the typical outcome. I want to start making cocktails at home beyond just vodka sodas but I don't want to buy a ton of random bottles right away. What's a small, versatile bar setup that lets me make a decent range of drinks?

This is a smart way to approach it, a lot of people either buy way too much specialty stuff upfront or stick to one spirit forever, and there's a well-established minimal setup that unlocks a genuinely wide range of classic cocktails without excessive investment. For spirits, a solid starting five: a good gin (versatile, works in a huge number of classics), a bourbon or rye whiskey, a blanco or reposado tequila, a white rum, and a good vodka if you still want that option, though vodka is honestly the least versatile of the group for classic cocktail-making specifically since it's designed to be relatively flavorless. The classic ratio is 2 parts rum, 1 part fresh lime juice, 3/4 part simple syrup (equal parts sugar and water, heated briefly to dissolve then cooled, keeps in the fridge for weeks), shaken hard with ice and strained into a chilled glass. The reason it's forgiving for a beginner despite only three ingredients is that the balance of sour, sweet, and strong is very intuitive to taste-test and adjust in real time, if it's too tart, add a touch more simple syrup, if it's too sweet, a touch more lime, there's no complex layering of multiple modifiers interacting in less obvious ways like a Manhattan or Negroni has, where vermouth, bitters, and spirit all shift the balance in less immediately obvious directions. One genuinely important tip regardless of which drink you start with: always use fresh-squeezed lime juice, never bottled lime juice concentrate, the difference in a Daiquiri specifically is enormous since fresh citrus has a brightness and complexity that bottled juice, which oxidizes and loses aromatic oils quickly after processing, simply can't replicate, this one substitution matters more than almost any other variable in determining whether your first attempts taste like a real cocktail or a flat, vaguely-limey sweet rum drink. Once the Daiquiri feels easy and well balanced, the Whiskey Sour uses a nearly identical ratio logic (spirit, citrus, sweetener) and is a natural next step before moving to drinks with vermouth or bitters layered in.
can you explain the core idea of stoicism in a way that's not just the marcus aurelius quote memes

The core of Stoic philosophy is the distinction between what is and isn't within your control, sometimes called the dichotomy of control. The Stoics argued that your judgments, intentions, desires, and reactions are up to you, while external events - other people's actions, your reputation, health, wealth, even the outcomes of your own efforts - are ultimately not fully within your control. Suffering, they argued, comes primarily from investing your sense of wellbeing in things outside that control, so the practical goal of Stoic training is to redirect your attention and effort toward the things you can actually govern, namely your own character and responses, and cultivate a kind of equanimity toward everything else. This isn't the popular caricature of just suppressing emotion or being stoic in the modern colloquial sense - it's a more active discipline of examining your judgments about events, since the Stoics held that it's not events themselves that disturb us but the judgments we form about them.
how is that different from just not caring about anything?

That's a common misreading. Stoicism doesn't ask you to stop caring about outcomes, it asks you to distinguish between the effort you put in, which is within your control and worth full commitment, and the outcome itself, which depends on factors beyond you. A Stoic archer, in a common analogy used by the school, aims and shoots with total focus and skill, but recognizes that a gust of wind or an unseen flaw in the target is outside their control, so their satisfaction should rest on having done the disciplined part well rather than purely on whether the arrow hits. That's a meaningfully different stance from indifference - it's actually a demanding standard for your own effort and character, paired with a deliberate release of attachment to what you can't govern.
I've always heard people say "the fall of Rome" like it was one single event, but I have a feeling it's more complicated than that. Can you actually explain what happened, in simple terms?

You're right to be suspicious of the single-event framing, it's genuinely one of the more misleading popular simplifications of history, historians today generally treat the "fall of Rome" as a long, gradual, multi-causal process spanning centuries rather than a single dramatic collapse, and even the specific date often cited, 476 CE, is really just the point when the last western Roman emperor was deposed, not a moment when Roman civilization or society itself abruptly ended. A useful starting distinction: the Roman Empire had split into a Western and Eastern half by the late 3rd/early 4th century for practical administrative reasons, since it had grown too large to govern effectively as one unit from a single capital. The Western Roman Empire is what most people mean by "the fall," and it did genuinely fragment and dissolve over the 5th century, under pressure from a combination of factors: repeated large-scale migrations and invasions by various groups (Visigoths, Vandals, and others) that the weakened western military increasingly couldn't repel, chronic internal political instability with frequent civil wars and rapid emperor turnover that undermined effective governance, and severe economic strain including debased currency and a shrinking tax base that made maintaining a large professional army and administration increasingly difficult over time. The Eastern Roman Empire, commonly called the Byzantine Empire by historians though its people still called themselves Romans, didn't fall in 476 at all, it continued for another thousand years, only finally ending when Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Empire in 1453, which is honestly the more surprising and less commonly known part of the story for most people.
Wait, a thousand more years is wild, I had no idea. Why does the popular narrative focus so heavily on 476 then if the empire really continued that long elsewhere?

That's a great question and it comes down to a mix of historical bias in how the story got written down over the centuries, plus which half of the empire had more lasting cultural influence on the parts of the world that later did most of the history-writing. A big part of it traces back to the Renaissance and Enlightenment era historians in Western Europe, particularly influential figures like Edward Gibbon writing in the 18th century, whose massive and hugely influential work "The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire" focused heavily on the western collapse as the dramatic centerpiece, partly because Western European scholars were naturally more interested in the history of their own geographic region's direct predecessor state, and partly because Gibbon's narrative fit a compelling storytelling arc, a great civilization's rise and tragic fall, that made for a more satisfying and widely read history than "actually it fragmented in the west but continued in a different form in the east for another millennium." Additionally, Western Europe underwent a very visible cultural and political discontinuity after the western collapse, feudalism, new Germanic kingdoms, Latin fragmenting into distinct Romance languages, which felt like an obvious dramatic break to later historians looking back, while the Eastern Empire's continuity felt, to Western-focused scholars, more like a curious footnote or a "different" empire (hence the somewhat externally imposed label "Byzantine," which its own people never actually used for themselves) rather than the real and legitimate continuation of Rome that it considered itself to be. Modern historians have increasingly pushed back on this western-centric framing, treating the Eastern Empire's long continuation as equally central to the "real" story of Rome's history, rather than a mere afterthought.

My piano teacher has me practicing scales every lesson and honestly it feels tedious and I don't really understand why they matter beyond just finger exercise. Can you explain what scales are actually building toward?

That tedium is a really common feeling, especially early on, since scales in isolation genuinely can feel like pure mechanical repetition without an obvious payoff, but they're actually building several distinct skills simultaneously that show up constantly once you're playing real music, even though the connection isn't always made explicit in lessons. First, physical technique: scales train consistent finger independence and evenness, including the tricky thumb-under and finger-over motions needed to smoothly cross your hand across the keyboard without looking, which shows up in essentially every piece of piano music beyond the most basic beginner pieces, any time a melodic line runs up or down more notes than you have fingers for one hand position, you're using scale technique whether the piece labels it that way or not. Second, and this is the part often undersold, scales build deep pattern recognition for music theory that dramatically speeds up learning new pieces later, once your hands and ears know what a G major scale feels and sounds like, sight-reading or memorizing a piece written in G major becomes noticeably faster since you're recognizing a familiar pattern rather than parsing each note as a brand new, unrelated fact. Third, scales build your ear's sense of key and tonality, helping you actually hear when a note sounds "right" or "wrong" within a piece, which is foundational for eventually being able to play by ear, improvise, or transpose music, skills that feel like a completely different, more advanced world early on but are directly built on the scale foundation you're currently finding tedious.
That actually makes the theory connection clearer. Is there a way to practice scales that's less mind numbing than just playing them straight up and down over and over?

Yes, and varying practice approach is honestly good advice regardless of tedium since different variations target genuinely different sub-skills, straight up-and-down repetition alone actually undertrains several useful things scales can build. Try rhythm variations: instead of playing every note the same even length, practice the same scale with a dotted rhythm (long-short, long-short alternating) or in groups of three with an accent on the first note of each group, this keeps your mind more actively engaged since you can't go on autopilot, while also building rhythmic control that transfers directly to actual pieces with syncopation or uneven rhythms. Try dynamic variations, playing the ascending half of the scale getting louder (crescendo) and the descending half getting softer (decrescendo), or the reverse, which builds genuine expressive control over touch and volume rather than just note accuracy, a skill that matters enormously in real musical performance but that pure mechanical scale practice, played at one flat volume, doesn't develop at all. Try scales in contrary motion, both hands starting on the same note and moving in opposite directions simultaneously, which is significantly more mentally engaging since your hands are doing mirror-image rather than identical motion, and builds a kind of bilateral coordination that parallel scale practice doesn't. Finally, try playing scales at a genuinely fast tempo you can barely control accurately, then slow back down, rather than always practicing at one comfortable medium speed, this trains your top-end technical ceiling in a way that plateaus faster if you never push tempo at all. Rotating through a few of these variations across different practice sessions, rather than always defaulting to plain straight repetition, tends to make the tedium noticeably more bearable while actually extracting more of the benefit scales are meant to provide in the first place.
what's the difference between "ambivalent" and "indifferent"? I keep mixing them up in writing

Easy mix-up because they both sound like 'not caring,' but they mean close to opposite things. Indifferent means you genuinely don't care either way — no strong feeling at all, low investment. Ambivalent means you have strong, conflicting feelings at the same time — you care a lot, but you're pulled in two directions. So "I'm ambivalent about the job offer" means part of you wants it and part of you doesn't, both strongly. "I'm indifferent to the job offer" means you basically don't have a preference either way. A quick test: if you could plausibly follow the sentence with 'on one hand... but on the other hand...', you mean ambivalent, not indifferent.

Glad it helped — it's one of those distinctions that's obvious once you have a concrete test, but easy to blur otherwise since both words get used loosely in casual speech.

My sourdough starter has been really sluggish the last week, barely doubling even after 8 hours. It smells fine, kind of tangy-sweet, no funky stuff. I keep it on the counter at room temp and feed it 1:1:1 once a day. Any idea what's going on?

First, room temperature matters a lot more than people expect: below about 70F, fermentation slows dramatically, so if your kitchen has cooled down recently (which happens a lot this time of year as seasons shift), that alone could explain sluggish rises. Try moving it somewhere warmer, like inside the microwave with the light on, near the fridge motor, or in an oven with just the light on for gentle warmth. Second, once-a-day 1:1:1 feeding might not be enough if your starter is very active and using up its food quickly, causing it to peak and fall before you check on it, which reads as sluggish when it's actually just past peak. Try feeding twice a day for a few days and see if that helps. Third, check your flour: if you switched flour brands or are using a very refined all-purpose with little bran/germ, the starter may have less to feed on. Adding a spoonful of whole wheat or rye to a feeding can give it a boost since those flours have more wild yeast and enzyme activity. Lastly, hydration ratio and container matter less but a loose lid trapping too much CO2 without any gas exchange can sometimes slow visible rise. Try a few of these and watch for a livelier rise within 2-3 days.

You can switch back all at once, there's no real need to taper it in. Starters are pretty resilient and will adjust to a flour change within one or two feeding cycles. Just do your next scheduled feeding with the better flour at your normal ratio, discard as usual, and watch the next rise. If you want a faster fix, you could also do one "boost" feeding with a higher proportion of whole grain flour, like a 1:1:1 ratio but subbing in 20-30% whole wheat or rye instead of all-purpose, which tends to wake up a lagging starter within a single feeding because of the extra nutrients and wild yeast population already present in whole grain flour. After that you can go back to your normal all-purpose routine. Keep an eye on rise times over the next two or three days; you should see it return to doubling within 4-6 hours if your kitchen is reasonably warm. If it's still lagging after that, temperature is probably the bigger factor and worth troubleshooting next.

what's the difference between a lookahead and a lookbehind in regex, and when would I actually use one

A lookahead, written (?=...) for positive or (?!...) for negative, checks what comes after the current position without consuming those characters. A lookbehind, (?<=...) or (?<!...), checks what comes before the current position, also without consuming it. Use case: say you want to match a number only when it's immediately followed by kg but you don't want kg included in the match - you'd write something like the digits followed by a positive lookahead for kg. If instead you want to match the text right after a dollar sign without including the sign itself, you'd use a lookbehind. They're handy whenever you need to assert context around a match without that context becoming part of the captured text.

Some lighter regex engines, like those used in certain older grep implementations or POSIX basic regex, don't support either lookahead or lookbehind at all. If portability matters, it's often safer to capture the surrounding context in a group and just discard it in post-processing rather than relying on lookaround.

what actually distinguishes baroque music from classical era music? they both sound kind of old-timey to me

The clearest structural difference is texture. Baroque music, roughly 1600 to 1750, favors polyphony and counterpoint - multiple independent melodic lines woven together, as in a Bach fugue, where several voices carry equally important material simultaneously. Classical era music, roughly 1750 to 1820, shifts toward homophony - a single clear melody supported by chordal accompaniment, which is why a lot of Mozart or early Beethoven sounds more like one singable tune with backing harmony rather than several competing melodic threads. Baroque music also tends to maintain one consistent mood or affect throughout a movement, called the doctrine of affections, while classical music introduces more dramatic contrast within a single movement, shifting between different themes and moods. Baroque keyboard music was largely written for harpsichord, which can't vary its dynamics by touch, while the classical era coincided with the rise of the piano, enabling the gradual dynamic shifts and expressive phrasing that became a hallmark of the style.

Once the piano became the dominant keyboard instrument, composers could write and rely on gradual dynamic swells as an expressive tool, and that capability fed directly into the classical style's preference for dramatic contrast and more continuously shaped phrasing within a movement.

what's the actual chemical difference between the fermentation that makes beer alcoholic and the one that makes yogurt sour?

They're driven by completely different organisms producing different end products from the same starting sugar. Beer fermentation is alcoholic fermentation, carried out by yeast, typically Saccharomyces cerevisiae, which converts glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide through glycolysis followed by the enzyme pathway that reduces pyruvate to acetaldehyde and then to ethanol, regenerating NAD+ in the process so glycolysis can keep running without oxygen. Yogurt fermentation is lactic acid fermentation, carried out by bacteria like Lactobacillus and Streptococcus thermophilus, which convert the lactose sugar in milk into lactic acid, again regenerating NAD+ but through a different single-step reduction of pyruvate directly to lactate rather than the two-step pathway to ethanol. The lactic acid buildup is what curdles the milk proteins and gives yogurt its characteristic tang, while in beer the ethanol and CO2 are the defining products, with the CO2 also responsible for carbonation if it's trapped during fermentation.
why does muscle tissue also do lactic acid fermentation during hard exercise then, is it using bacteria?

No bacteria involved there - it's your own muscle cells running the same basic anaerobic fallback pathway, just without any microorganisms. When oxygen supply can't keep up with ATP demand during intense exercise, muscle cells can't run oxidative phosphorylation fast enough, so they shift to anaerobic glycolysis, and just like in the yogurt bacteria, they need to regenerate NAD+ to keep glycolysis running, which they do by converting pyruvate into lactate via the same type of enzyme, lactate dehydrogenase. It's essentially the same core biochemical solution to the same underlying problem, run independently by two very different kinds of cells that both need to keep glycolysis functioning without oxygen.
What were the main structural reasons the Roman Republic collapsed, beyond just Caesar crossing the Rubicon?

The Rubicon moment was really the culmination of decades of structural strain rather than a sudden cause. A few big threads: first, the Republic's institutions were designed for a city-state, not the sprawling Mediterranean empire Rome had become by the 2nd century BCE - governors and generals far from Rome accumulated personal power and loyal armies that owed more to them than to the state. Second, the Marian reforms professionalized the army and tied soldiers' loyalty to their commanders, who promised land and pay, rather than to the Senate - this made generals like Sulla, Pompey, and Caesar into independent power brokers with private armies. Third, growing economic inequality - cheap slave labor from conquests undercut small farmers, who lost land and flooded into Rome, creating a volatile urban poor that populist politicians could mobilize. Finally, the Senate's own conservatism and unwillingness to reform (the failed attempts by the Gracchi brothers to redistribute land are a good example) meant grievances built up with no institutional outlet, so they got resolved through violence and civil war instead.

But the deeper structural issues, like provincial governance and army loyalty, wouldn't have been touched by land reform alone, so it likely would have delayed rather than prevented the eventual crisis.
I'm trying to write a villanelle but keep messing up the repeating line structure, can you explain it simply and maybe give a mini example

The structure: 19 lines total, five tercets (3-line stanzas) plus a final quatrain (4-line stanza). Two lines from the first stanza repeat throughout: line 1 (call it A1) and line 3 (call it A2). A1 repeats as the last line of stanzas 2 and 4; A2 repeats as the last line of stanzas 3 and 5. In the final quatrain, both A1 and A2 appear together as the last two lines. The rhyme scheme is ABA for each tercet and ABAA for the closing quatrain (using the same A and B sounds throughout the whole poem).

Here's a mini (non-full-length, just illustrating the pattern) three-stanza fragment:

Stanza 1:
The tide keeps time the way the shore forgets. (A1)
Each wave arrives and leaves without a name. (B)
I count the hours the ocean never sets. (A2)

Stanza 2:
The gulls repeat what no one quite regrets. (A)
Salt in the wind, and nothing stays the same. (B)
The tide keeps time the way the shore forgets. (A1 repeats)

That pattern of A1/A2 alternating as stanza-enders is really the whole trick — once you have those two lines locked in from stanza one, the rest of the poem is built around returning to them.

That's exactly the common mistake — it's an easy one to make since the form is unusual. Alternating them (A1 at the end of stanza 2, A2 at the end of stanza 3, A1 again at stanza 4, A2 again at stanza 5) is what gives a villanelle its slow-build, circling feeling rather than just being repetitive. Good luck with the rest of it.

why does atomic radius decrease as you go across a period but increase down a group?

Across a period, you're adding protons to the nucleus while electrons are being added to the same outer shell, so the increasing positive nuclear charge pulls that outer shell in more tightly without adding a new layer of shielding - the net effect is a stronger effective pull on the outer electrons, shrinking the radius. Down a group, each successive element adds a whole new electron shell further from the nucleus, and while the nuclear charge does increase, the additional inner shells shield the outer electrons from much of that charge, so the outer shell ends up both farther away and less tightly held, making the atom larger overall.
does ionization energy follow the same pattern then?

Yes, and it makes sense given the same underlying logic - ionization energy generally increases across a period because the outer electrons are held more tightly by that stronger effective nuclear pull, so it takes more energy to remove one. Down a group, ionization energy generally decreases because the outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so it's held more loosely and easier to remove. There are some exceptions and small dips within periods due to subshell stability effects, but the broad trend tracks directly with the atomic radius trend.

I've been doing Duolingo for Spanish for 6 months and I feel like I know a lot of words but can't actually hold a conversation. What am I missing?

The fix is deliberately practicing output under time pressure rather than more input accumulation. A few concrete changes: start doing italki or similar tutoring sessions, even just 30 minutes a week with a conversation-focused tutor, since nothing replicates the pressure and unpredictability of real conversation like an actual conversation, apps simply can't simulate the need to formulate a response in real time to something you didn't expect. Second, practice thinking in Spanish during small daily moments, narrating your actions internally in simple Spanish while making coffee or driving, which builds the retrieval speed that conversation requires without needing a partner every time. I noticed tiny white fuzzy spots on my pothos, kind of like little cotton balls clustered near the stem joints. Is this a disease or a bug, and how do I get rid of it?

That description, small white cottony clusters specifically near stem joints and leaf junctions, is a very classic description of mealybugs, a common houseplant pest, not a disease, and the good news is they're very treatable if caught reasonably early like it sounds like you have. Mealybugs are small soft-bodied insects that cover themselves in a white, waxy, cotton-like secretion for protection, which is exactly what you're seeing clustered in those joint areas, they specifically favor these hidden, protected nooks because it's harder for predators, and your inspection, to spot them there. First step, isolate the plant from any others nearby immediately, mealybugs spread readily to neighboring plants through contact or even just proximity, so this prevents a small problem becoming a whole-collection problem while you treat it. Treatment: dip a cotton swab in rubbing alcohol (isopropyl, 70% is fine) and directly dab each visible cluster, the alcohol dissolves their protective waxy coating and kills them on contact quite effectively, do a full pass over the entire plant, checking undersides of leaves and all stem joints carefully since they hide well. Follow this a few days later with a full plant treatment of insecticidal soap or neem oil spray, covering the whole plant thoroughly including leaf undersides, since alcohol swabbing handles what's visible but eggs or newly hatched nymphs you missed can repopulate if you don't follow up with a broader treatment.
How many rounds of treatment should I expect to need before it's actually fully gone, and how do I know when it's safe to put the plant back near my others?

Mealybugs are persistent specifically because their eggs are protected and can hatch in waves over several weeks, so a single treatment, even a thorough one, usually isn't sufficient, plan on a repeating treatment cycle rather than a one-time fix. A typical realistic timeline: do the alcohol swab plus full neem oil or insecticidal soap spray treatment as your first round, then repeat the full spray treatment every 7-10 days for at least 3-4 rounds total, even if the plant looks clean after just one or two rounds, since newly hatched nymphs from eggs that survived the first treatment often aren't visible yet but will appear within that timeframe if you stop too early. Continue this cycle until you've had at least two consecutive treatment checks, roughly 2-3 weeks, with zero new mealybugs spotted anywhere on the plant, including a close inspection of stem joints, leaf undersides, and even the soil surface where they can sometimes hide near the base. For safely reintroducing it to your other plants, I'd be conservative given how easily these spread, keep it isolated for the full duration of treatment, and only reintroduce it after that clean 2-3 week stretch with no new sightings across multiple inspections, not just after the first treatment looks successful. While it's isolated, it's also worth doing a one-time close inspection of the plants that were previously near it, just to catch any early spread you might have missed before isolating, since a few days or weeks of proximity before you noticed the infestation is enough time for mealybugs to have potentially moved to a neighboring plant already.

The good news is that a genuinely great best man speech doesn't actually require being naturally funny, the speeches people remember fondly are almost always the sincere, specific ones, not the ones trying hardest to be a comedy routine, so reframing your goal away from "be funny" and toward "be genuine and specific" will actually make this both easier and more likely to land well. Start by collecting raw material before worrying about structure at all: write down, without judging any of it yet, several specific memories of your brother, moments that show who he really is, a time he showed you kindness, something that captures his personality well, how he talks about his now-spouse, a moment you realized this relationship was different or serious for him. Specific, concrete details beat generic sentiment every time, "he's always been a great brother" lands flat, while a specific small story that shows he's a great brother, without ever stating it outright, lands much harder because the audience draws the conclusion themselves rather than being told. A reliable structure once you have your material: a brief, warm opening (who you are and your relationship to the groom, kept short), one or two well-chosen stories or memories about your brother, ideally including at least one lighter, warm moment even if it's not a big joke, just genuine affection often gets a warm laugh on its own, a section that specifically addresses the couple together, what you've observed about them as partners, why you're happy for this marriage, and a closing toast, a simple sincere line wishing them well followed by "raise your glasses" cueing everyone to stand and toast.
That helps a lot actually. How long should it be, and any tips for actually not freezing up when I'm standing there in front of everyone?

Length-wise, 3 to 5 minutes is the standard sweet spot for a best man speech, which usually works out to somewhere around 500-750 spoken words depending on your pace, long enough to include a real story or two with some substance, short enough that it doesn't become a strain on the room's attention or turn into a rambling ordeal, when in doubt, especially given your stated nervousness, err on the shorter side, a tight 3 minute speech that lands well beats a meandering 6 minute one every time. For the freezing-up fear specifically, a few practical things that genuinely help beyond just "practice more." Print your speech in a large, easy to read font and bring the physical paper with you even if you've mostly memorized it, having it as a visible safety net dramatically reduces anxiety since you know you can never be truly lost, even a brief mental blank becomes a quick glance down rather than a panic spiral. On the actual day, before you're called up, do a minute of slow breathing with a longer exhale than inhale, this genuinely calms the physical adrenaline response, and remind yourself that everyone in that room is actively rooting for you to succeed, a wedding audience is about as warm and forgiving an audience as exists for a nervous speaker, nobody there wants you to fail or is judging small stumbles harshly, they're there to celebrate your brother and will be moved by your sincerity far more than by polished delivery.

why did linear perspective specifically emerge in renaissance italy? was nobody drawing depth before that?

Artists before the Renaissance absolutely tried to convey depth, but earlier techniques like overlapping figures, varying size somewhat intuitively, or medieval hierarchical scaling, where important figures like saints were drawn larger regardless of actual distance, weren't built on a consistent mathematical system. Linear perspective as a systematic, geometrically grounded technique is usually credited to the architect Filippo Brunelleschi in early 15th century Florence, who demonstrated that a scene's depth could be constructed by having parallel lines converge toward a single vanishing point on the horizon, mirroring how the eye actually perceives receding parallel lines like a road or a row of columns. Leon Battista Alberti then formalized this into a written treatise, giving other artists a reproducible method rather than an intuitive trick. It emerged specifically in Renaissance Florence partly because of the era's broader intellectual climate blending art with mathematics and optics, revived interest in classical Greek and Roman ideas about geometry, and patronage from wealthy families and guilds eager to fund ambitious architectural and artistic projects that rewarded this kind of technical innovation.
did that mathematical approach change how artists were trained after that, or was it more of a niche technique some used?

It became foundational fairly quickly, at least in Italy and then across Europe. Once linear perspective was formalized, it got incorporated into workshop training as a core technical skill alongside anatomy and proportion, since it gave artists a reliable method for constructing believable architectural spaces and figure placement rather than relying purely on instinct. Within a couple of generations it was assumed knowledge for any ambitious painter, and treatises on perspective, proportion, and anatomy became standard parts of an artist's theoretical education, reflecting the Renaissance ideal of the artist as someone versed in both craft and scientific principles rather than purely a manual craftsman.

I've started doing the daily crossword but I only ever finish the easy Monday ones, by Thursday and Friday I'm completely lost. What separates easy puzzles from hard ones beyond just harder vocabulary?

Vocabulary difficulty is actually one of the smaller factors, the real difference between early-week and late-week puzzles, at least in the standard American crossword convention where difficulty increases through the week, mostly comes down to clue style rather than the words themselves being genuinely more obscure. Monday and Tuesday puzzles use mostly straightforward, literal clues, a clue like "Feline pet" for CAT means exactly what it says. By Thursday and especially Friday and Saturday, clues shift heavily toward wordplay, misdirection, and clues that require lateral thinking rather than direct definition. Common late-week clue types worth learning to recognize: clues ending in a question mark almost always signal a pun or wordplay twist rather than a literal definition, so "Something you might spot on a leopard? (informal)" is playing with a double meaning, not asking about spot markings literally. Clues that seem to be about one specific, narrow topic are often actually a broader category in disguise, requiring you to think about what category the specific example belongs to rather than the specific thing itself. Anagram indicators (words like "scrambled," "confused," "mixed up") signal that letters in the clue itself need rearranging to form the answer. Abbreviation and cross-reference clues become much more common late week too, referencing other clue numbers in the grid, which early week puzzles rarely use. Late-week puzzles also lean much more heavily on general pop culture, wordplay-based humor, and clues assuming a shared cultural knowledge base rather than dictionary-style factual knowledge, which is why raw vocabulary study alone doesn't close the gap as much as learning the actual clue-solving patterns does.
The question mark thing is useful to know. Is there a good way to actually practice recognizing these patterns, or does it just come with doing enough puzzles over time?

It does improve naturally with volume over time, but you can meaningfully accelerate that process with a few more deliberate practices rather than just passively hoping repetition alone does the work. First, when you finish a puzzle, whether you solved it fully or had to look up some answers, go back through the clues you found hardest or got wrong and specifically analyze the wordplay mechanism being used, ask "what type of trick was this clue using" rather than just moving on once you know the answer, explicitly categorizing the trick (pun, hidden word, anagram, double definition) builds a mental catalog of patterns much faster than solving alone without this reflection step. Second, work backward from solutions occasionally, take a puzzle you've already completed, cover the answers, and specifically try to figure out why a tricky clue leads to its answer, reverse-engineering the logic of clues you already know the answer to is a lower-pressure way to build pattern recognition than always working forward under time pressure while also trying to solve. Third, consider working through puzzles slightly below your current struggle level with a focus on late-week style specifically, rather than jumping straight to the hardest puzzles, some crossword apps and books specifically compile "trickiest clue types" collections aimed at exactly this kind of skill-building, working through a themed collection of similar difficulty level repeatedly reinforces the same pattern types until they click. Fourth, don't discount just doing the puzzle you're stuck on with a partner or solving community, discussing why a particular clue works with someone more experienced, or reading online explanations for late-week puzzles after attempting them (many crossword blogs post daily explainer posts breaking down each clue's wordplay), accelerates pattern learning significantly compared to solving in isolation without ever seeing the reasoning behind clues you couldn't crack on your own.

There's a ballot measure in a nearby city about piloting a universal basic income program and it's become a huge local debate. I go back and forth on whether it would actually work or just cause problems like inflation or people quitting jobs. What does the actual evidence say?

The evidence from pilot programs that have actually been run is more nuanced than either side of the debate usually presents it. Several city-level pilots in different countries have generally found that recipients don't dramatically drop out of the workforce the way critics predicted, though there is often a modest reduction in hours worked, particularly among people using the extra security to search for a better job fit rather than settling for whatever was available, or to care for family members. Mental health and financial stress indicators tend to improve fairly consistently across these pilots too, which supporters point to as a meaningful benefit even if it's harder to put a clean dollar value on than employment statistics.
That's more encouraging than I expected honestly. What about the inflation concern, is that a real risk or mostly overstated?

It's a legitimate theoretical concern, but the localized pilots run so far haven't been large enough in scale to really test it, since a small city-level program doesn't inject enough new spending into a broad enough economy to meaningfully move prices the way a full national rollout might. Economists who study this generally agree the inflation risk becomes more serious the larger and more universal the program gets, especially if it's funded by simply creating new money rather than through redistribution from taxation, since the latter doesn't necessarily increase the total amount of money circulating in the economy, it just shifts who holds it. So the honest answer is that current pilot evidence can't fully settle the inflation question one way or the other, since it's mostly been tested at a scale too small to reveal that particular risk.
That distinction between funding through new money versus redistribution is helpful, I hadn't thought about that as a separate variable from the basic income question itself.

It's honestly one of the most underappreciated parts of the debate, since people often argue about basic income as if it's one single policy, when in practice the funding mechanism matters just as much as the payment structure itself. A basic income funded through a tax on land value or a carbon tax has very different economic effects than one funded through deficit spending, even if the amount each recipient gets is identical. It might be worth digging into how your local ballot measure specifically proposes to fund it, since that detail probably tells you more about the likely real world effects than the basic income concept itself does.
How significant was the printing press really, compared to other medieval technologies?

It's hard to overstate. Before Gutenberg's movable-type press around 1440, books were copied by hand, which made them expensive, slow to produce, and limited mostly to monasteries, universities, and the wealthy. A single scribe might take months to copy one book. The printing press collapsed both the cost and time of reproduction by orders of magnitude - within 50 years, tens of millions of books had been printed across Europe. That had cascading effects: it accelerated the spread of the Reformation since Luther's writings could be mass-distributed almost immediately, standardized spelling and grammar across regions as printed texts became reference points, and fueled the Scientific Revolution by letting researchers share and verify findings much faster than hand-copied manuscripts allowed. Compared to something like the mechanical clock or the compass, which mainly changed specific domains, the printing press reshaped how information itself moved through society.
did literacy rates actually jump quickly after that or did it take a long time

It took a while - printing made books cheaper and more available, but literacy growth lagged behind by a couple of centuries in most of Europe, since access to books doesn't automatically translate into people being taught to read, and formal education systems were still limited. Widespread literacy really only started climbing significantly from the 17th century onward, especially in Protestant regions where reading the Bible directly was encouraged, and it wasn't until the 19th century with public schooling movements that literacy rates in much of Europe approached majority levels.

I want to start meal prepping vegetarian lunches for the work week but every time I try, by Thursday everything tastes the same and I'm sick of it. How do people actually make prepped food not boring?

The Thursday fatigue almost always comes from prepping one complete dish five times rather than prepping modular components you recombine differently each day, which is the actual trick professional meal preppers use. Instead of making, say, five containers of the same vegetable stir fry, prep separate components in bulk: one grain (rice, farro, or quinoa), one or two protein sources (roasted chickpeas, baked tofu, black beans), three or four vegetables roasted or sauteed separately so their flavors stay distinct, and two or three different sauces or dressings in small jars, like a tahini lemon sauce, a spicy peanut sauce, and a basic vinaigrette. Then each day you assemble a different combination, grain plus chickpeas plus roasted broccoli plus tahini sauce on Monday, same grain plus black beans plus roasted peppers plus peanut sauce on Tuesday, and suddenly it feels like different meals even though the shopping and cooking effort was the same as making one dish five times. Varying the sauce alone does most of the heavy lifting here since sauce is what your palate registers most strongly. Also prep in appropriately different textures, something crunchy like toasted nuts or seeds sprinkled on top at the end of each meal (not prepped soggy in advance) keeps things interesting texturally even when the base ingredients repeat.
That's a good system. Do you have go-to sauce recipes that keep well in the fridge for the week?

Yes, a few reliable ones that hold up for 5-7 days refrigerated without separating badly or losing flavor. Tahini lemon sauce: whisk together a quarter cup tahini, juice of one lemon, one minced garlic clove, a splash of water to thin, and salt to taste, it'll thicken in the fridge so just add a little water to loosen before using. Spicy peanut sauce: combine a quarter cup peanut butter, two tablespoons soy sauce, one tablespoon rice vinegar, one teaspoon sriracha or chili garlic sauce, one teaspoon honey or maple syrup, and enough warm water to thin to a pourable consistency, this one is very forgiving and keeps well over a week. A basic miso vinaigrette: whisk one tablespoon white miso paste with two tablespoons rice vinegar, one tablespoon neutral oil, and a teaspoon of sesame oil, great over roasted vegetables and grains for a different flavor profile than the other two. A simple green herb sauce, blending cilantro or parsley with lime juice, olive oil, garlic, and a pinch of salt, adds brightness that cuts through heavier grain bowls and also keeps roughly a week if you add a thin layer of oil on top to limit oxidation. Rotating between these four alone, on the same base ingredients, gives you enough variety that a five day prep genuinely doesn't feel repetitive by Thursday.

I'm trying to write haiku for the first time beyond the 5-7-5 syllable thing I learned in school. What actually makes a haiku good versus just a syllable-counting exercise?

The syllable count is honestly the least important part, and traditional Japanese haiku don't even map cleanly onto English syllables since the original mora-counting system doesn't translate directly, which is why a lot of serious English-language haiku poets treat 5-7-5 as a loose guideline rather than a strict rule. What actually makes a haiku work is usually three things. First, a kireji or "cutting" moment, a juxtaposition between two images or ideas that creates a spark of meaning in the gap between them, rather than one continuous descriptive sentence. Classic haiku often present an image, then pivot to a second, seemingly unrelated image, and the reader's mind does the work of connecting them, which is where the emotional or philosophical resonance comes from. Second, concrete sensory imagery over abstraction, naming a specific bird, a specific quality of light, a specific sound, rather than vague emotional statements like "I feel sad" or "nature is beautiful." Third, a seasonal or temporal anchor, called kigo in the Japanese tradition, something that locates the poem in a specific moment of the year or day, which grounds the abstract feeling in a real, physical world. A haiku succeeds when it captures a single, sharp moment of perception rather than trying to narrate or explain, leaving space for the reader to feel the connection rather than being told it.
Can you show me an example of the juxtaposition technique, maybe with a fall theme since that fits the season right now?

Sure, here's one built around that cutting technique: "porch light left on / a single moth circles once / then finds the dark yard" The first line sets a small, ordinary domestic image, a porch light, something warm and human. The second line introduces the moth, drawn to that light as expected. The turn happens in the third line: rather than the moth staying at the light as convention would predict, it circles once and leaves for the dark yard instead, which creates a small but real emotional gap for the reader to fill, maybe about restlessness, or choosing solitude over comfort, or simply the unpredictability of small creatures, the poem doesn't say which, and that's intentional. Notice there's no explanation, no "and this made me think about," the juxtaposition itself carries the meaning. Another version leaning harder into a seasonal kigo: "first frost on the fence / my father's coat, still on its hook / by the door" this pairs a seasonal, natural image (first frost) with a very specific, small human object (a coat on a hook), and the emotional weight, likely about someone gone or distant, comes entirely from the reader connecting those two images rather than from any stated feeling. When you draft your own, try writing the two images completely separately first, unrelated notes about things you noticed today, then look for an unexpected pairing between any two of them, that's usually a faster path to a real cut than trying to force one image to naturally lead to another.

My closet is completely overwhelming, I have way too many clothes and I don't even wear most of them but I freeze up every time I try to declutter and end up keeping everything anyway. What's a system that actually works instead of just "if it doesn't spark joy"?

The freeze-up you're describing is really common and it usually comes from trying to make an emotionally loaded judgment call, do I love this, will I regret this, on every single item simultaneously, which is mentally exhausting and leads to decision fatigue that resolves itself by defaulting to "keep everything" just to make the discomfort stop. A more mechanical, less emotionally taxing system tends to work better for people who get stuck this way. Try the hanger trick as a starting data-gathering phase before making any keep/discard decisions at all: turn every hanger in your closet backwards (hook facing out instead of the normal direction), and for the next 30-60 days, every time you actually wear something, return it to the closet with the hanger facing the normal direction. After that period, look at what's still facing backwards, that's your genuinely unused clothing, based on real behavior rather than a hypothetical guess about whether you might wear something someday, this removes the emotional guessing entirely since you're just observing actual data about your real habits rather than making a values judgment on each item in the moment. For the actual decluttering session once you have that data, use a strict three-pile system rather than an open-ended judgment call: keep, donate, and a small "maybe" box that gets sealed, dated, and put away out of sight for 3-6 months, if you never go looking for anything in that box during that period, it gets donated unopened when the date arrives, without reopening it and re-litigating each item, this gives your anxious "but what if I need it" brain a safety net that makes letting go of "maybe" items feel much less final and scary in the moment.
The maybe box makes sense but I'm worried I'll just keep everything in the maybe pile and never actually get rid of anything. How do I stop that from happening?

That's a fair worry and a genuinely common failure mode of the maybe-box system if it's not paired with some structure, the fix is putting a hard constraint on the maybe pile itself rather than leaving it open-ended, since an unlimited maybe pile just becomes a second closet you're avoiding rather than actually solving anything. Set a firm size limit before you start, literally one specific box or bin, not "a pile," a physical container with a fixed size, and the rule is once it's full, anything else uncertain has to go directly to donate, not into some second overflow maybe container, this forces genuine triage rather than letting the maybe category expand indefinitely to absorb everything you're unsure about. When something new comes up for the maybe pile and the box is already full, make yourself directly compare it against what's currently sitting in the box, if it wouldn't beat out the least-certain item already in there, it goes to donate instead, this comparative approach is psychologically easier than an absolute judgment ("is this worth keeping, yes or no") since relative comparisons are something the brain handles with much less friction and hesitation than absolute ones. Also, genuinely commit to the sealed, dated aspect, actually tape the box shut and write the reopen date on it in marker, and put it somewhere slightly inconvenient, a high shelf or storage area, not conveniently back in your closet, since easy access defeats the entire purpose of the exercise, which is letting time and real behavior, not another anxious in-the-moment decision, make the final call for you. Most people who follow through on the full sealed period find they don't even remember what's in the box by the time the date arrives, which is itself pretty strong evidence for how little they'd have actually missed those items had they donated them immediately in the first place.

I wrote a short story about a lighthouse keeper who starts hearing his dead wife's voice in the foghorn. It's 2000 words. I feel like the ending is too abrupt, he just walks into the sea. Any thoughts on how to fix pacing without adding a ton of length?

An abrupt ending after a slow, atmospheric build usually means the emotional turn needs one more beat before the final action, not more description. Right now the jump from "hearing her voice" to "walks into the sea" probably reads as a leap in logic to the reader even if it feels inevitable to you as the writer. Consider adding a short scene, even just 150-250 words, where he actively resists or rationalizes the pull, like turning away from the water once, going back inside, trying to drown out the foghorn some mundane way, failing. That single moment of resistance and failure gives the ending weight because we see him lose a fight, not just have a compulsion. You could also plant one earlier, tiny detail that pays off in the final image, like an object of hers he's been avoiding touching that he finally picks up right before he walks out. That kind of callback creates a sense of closure and inevitability without needing extra pages of new content. Also check whether the final paragraph lingers a beat too long or cuts a beat too short: abrupt endings are often actually well-timed but under-earned, meaning the content before them didn't do enough work, rather than the ending itself being wrong.
That's helpful. Do you think the foghorn as her voice is too on the nose as a symbol?

It's a well worn image, but well worn doesn't mean it can't work, it depends on execution and whether you lean into or subvert the expectation. The risk with a foghorn-as-dead-wife's-voice symbol is that readers who've encountered lighthouse grief stories before will see the metaphor coming from the first page and then just wait for the story to catch up to what they already know, which flattens tension. A few ways to freshen it: make the voice ambiguous for longer, so the reader isn't sure if it's really her, grief hallucination, or something supernatural, and let the keeper's own uncertainty drive tension rather than the reader's certainty. Alternatively, subvert it by having the foghorn's meaning shift over the story, starting as comfort, then obligation, then finally something he needs to silence to move on, which uses the same central image but avoids it being static and predictable. Another option is undercutting the symbol with something mundane and specific, like her actual voice used a phrase or laugh that the foghorn's rhythm coincidentally echoes, which grounds the supernatural feeling in a very personal, non-generic detail rather than a universal grief cliche. Any of these would let you keep the foghorn but make it feel earned rather than obvious.
I keep seeing "rate limiting" mentioned in API documentation and error messages but I don't have a solid grasp on what it actually means or why services do it. Can you explain the concept simply?

Rate limiting is essentially a policy a service puts in place that restricts how many requests a given client (a user, an API key, an IP address) can make within a certain time window, for example "100 requests per minute" or "1000 requests per day," and if you exceed that threshold, the service will reject additional requests, usually returning a specific error response (very commonly HTTP status code 429, "Too Many Requests") until the time window resets or enough time passes. The core reasons services implement this fall into a few main categories. Protecting infrastructure and stability: without limits, a single client, whether through a bug in their own code, a traffic spike, or actual malicious intent, could send an overwhelming volume of requests that degrades performance for every other user of the service, rate limiting acts as a safety valve ensuring fair, predictable access for everyone rather than one client accidentally or deliberately monopolizing shared server resources. Cost management: many services incur real infrastructure or downstream costs per request, especially anything that triggers expensive computation or calls to other paid services internally, so limiting request volume directly controls their own operating costs and prevents abuse that could otherwise run up unexpected bills. Business model enforcement: many APIs offer tiered pricing, a free tier with a low rate limit and paid tiers with progressively higher limits, using rate limits as the actual mechanism that differentiates and enforces those pricing tiers rather than relying purely on trust or a separate billing system for every single request.
If I'm building something that calls an API a lot, what's the standard way to actually handle rate limit errors gracefully in my own code rather than just crashing or spamming retries?

The standard, widely recommended pattern is called exponential backoff, ideally combined with jitter, and it's specifically designed to handle exactly this situation gracefully rather than either giving up immediately or hammering the API with rapid retries that would just extend the problem. The core idea: when you receive a rate limit error (that 429 status code), don't retry immediately, instead wait a short delay, then retry, and if you get rate limited again, double (or otherwise increase) that delay before the next attempt, repeating this pattern up to some reasonable maximum number of attempts or maximum total delay, rather than retrying at a fixed interval or, worse, retrying in a tight loop with no delay at all, which is the single most common beginner mistake and one that often gets an API key or IP address more aggressively or permanently blocked, since it looks like abusive or malicious traffic to the service, rather than a legitimate application handling a temporary limit. Jitter means adding a small random variation to each delay, rather than a perfectly predictable doubling sequence, this matters more when many clients might be retrying simultaneously (like many users of your app all hitting a rate limit around the same time), since without jitter, all those clients would retry at exactly the same synchronized moments, potentially causing repeated collision spikes, while randomized jitter spreads those retries out more naturally. Many good API clients also respect a "Retry-After" header if the service provides one in its 429 response, which tells you explicitly how long to wait rather than guessing, and you should always prefer that explicit signal over your own backoff calculation when it's available, since the service itself knows its exact reset timing better than any external guess could. Most mature HTTP client libraries have this backoff-with-jitter retry logic available as a built-in or easily added feature, rather than needing to hand-roll it yourself from scratch, which is worth checking before writing custom retry logic.

I've tried to start journaling like five separate times and always quit within two weeks. I want it to stick this time. What usually makes journaling habits fail and how do I avoid that?

The most common failure pattern is starting with too much ambition, both in format and frequency, treating journaling as a substantial daily writing task (a full page, deep reflective prose, every single day without fail) rather than as a small, flexible habit that can flex with your actual energy and time on any given day. When the ambitious version inevitably gets skipped once or twice due to a busy day, most people experience that as a failure of the whole habit rather than a normal blip, and quit entirely rather than just resuming smaller the next day. A better structural approach: pick a genuinely tiny minimum version you'd do even on your worst day, like three bullet points, no full sentences required, something as simple as one good thing, one hard thing, one thing you're looking forward to, this should feel almost embarrassingly easy to do, which is the point, since consistency matters far more than depth for actually building the habit long term. Attach it to an existing routine rather than relying on remembering, right after brushing your teeth, or right when you sit down with morning coffee, habit stacking onto something you already do reliably every day removes the need for willpower or memory to trigger it. And build in explicit permission to skip a day without it meaning failure, missing one day and resuming the next is completely different from quitting, but a lot of people's black-and-white thinking treats any gap as proof the habit "didn't work," when in reality nearly everyone's real habits have occasional gaps.

what were impressionist painters actually rebelling against? I know it was a big deal at the time but not why

They were reacting against the strict standards of the official French Academy, which controlled the prestigious Salon exhibitions and favored highly finished, smooth-surfaced paintings of historical, mythological, or religious subjects, typically composed and painted carefully in a studio rather than outdoors. Painters like Monet, Renoir, and Degas instead wanted to capture fleeting, everyday moments and the actual sensory experience of light and atmosphere as it changed from minute to minute, which pushed them to paint outdoors, a practice called en plein air, often working quickly with visible, loose brushstrokes and unmixed colors placed side by side rather than smoothly blended, letting the viewer's eye do some of the optical blending. This was considered radical and unfinished-looking by Academy standards, and their unofficial exhibitions, held independently after the Academy repeatedly rejected their work, were initially mocked by critics, with the term impressionism itself originating as a somewhat derisive reference to Monet's painting Impression, Sunrise, implying the work looked like a rough sketch rather than a completed piece.
did the Academy's rejection actually hurt their careers financially at the time or did they do okay?

It took roughly a couple of decades before Impressionism moved from being ridiculed to being commercially successful and critically respected, and by the later part of their careers many of the major Impressionists, particularly Monet, did become quite financially successful, but that reversal came only after a long stretch of being considered outsiders by the mainstream art establishment.
